propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of the RAD decision affirming the RPD decision denying refugee status.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a decision by the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD], dated September 17, 2021, affirming a decision of the Refugee Protection Division [RPD], which found the Applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of the RAD decision affirming the RPD decision denying refugee status.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a Chinese citizen fearing persecution by the PSB for political opinion after protesting farmland expropriation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of China. He fears persecution from the Public Security Bureau [PSB] due to his political opinion after he was targeted for protesting what he considered the unfair expropriation of his farmland in his village.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a Chinese citizen fearing PSB persecution for protesting farmland expropriation.

propositions.text: Applicant leased orchard land in 2013; in 2017 government ordered expropriation for high-rise construction and terminated leases; compensation offered was unacceptable.
propositions.quote: In 2013 he started his own orchard business on a 15 year lease. However, in 2017 the local government provided notice to him and 19 other farms their land must be expropriated so high-rise structures could be built. The Applicant was, therefore, given an order that his lease agreement was to be terminated. The government offered some compensation to affected households, but the Applicant and his wife found this amount unacceptable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's orchard lease was terminated in 2017 for expropriation; compensation was unacceptable to him and his wife.

propositions.text: Farmers chose representatives to meet government in Sept 2018; government insisted project proceed and land be expropriated before deadline; follow-ups failed.
propositions.quote: After meeting with other farmers, representatives were chosen to speak with the government and seek a resolution. In September 2018, the chosen representatives attended the local government and met with a high-ranking official. Ultimately, they were told that the project must be carried on and land expropriated before the deadline. They followed up several times with no success.

paragraphs.summary: The court states farmers' representatives met government in 2018 but were told expropriation would proceed; follow-ups were unsuccessful.

propositions.text: Farmers went to local People’s Congress, were redirected to local government, then decided to organize a public demonstration due to frustration.
propositions.quote: The group subsequently went to the local People’s Congress and were told they would receive and answer soon, but were redirected to the local government once again. With frustrations rising, the group decided to organize a public demonstration.

paragraphs.summary: The court states farmers were redirected from People’s Congress to local government and then decided to protest publicly due to frustration.

propositions.text: In fall 2017, about 20 villagers including Applicant protested outside local government with banners and slogans; group grew to about 100 people.
propositions.quote: In the fall of 2017, the group organized about 20 villagers, including the Applicant, to demonstrate outside the local government. The protestors stood outside the entry of the building, held banners and shouted slogans regarding corruption. The Applicant stood beside the three main representatives at the front of the group and shouted slogans. The protestors swelled to a group of about 100 people.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant joined a protest in fall 2017 that grew to about 100 people with banners and slogans.

propositions.text: Local government led protestors inside to negotiate; PSB officers detained them and threatened Applicant to stop anti-government protests with severe consequences.
propositions.quote: The local Government led the protestors, including the Applicant, into the building to negotiate. However, shortly thereafter PSB officers rushed into the room and detained them for questioning. The PSB officers demanded that the Applicant “stop organizing and protesting in any anti-government demonstration.” The Applicant was then allegedly threatened with “severe consequences” if he continued to protest.

paragraphs.summary: The court states protestors were detained by PSB officers who threatened the Applicant to stop anti-government protests.

propositions.text: Protestors released after one night; Applicant vowed to continue; on way to provincial government, bus stopped by PSB and detained for four nights.
propositions.quote: After spending one night in detention, the protestors were released. In meeting with the representatives after the meeting, the Applicant declared that he would not give up. The representatives agreed and decided to go to the provincial government for assistance. On their way, the bus was stopped on the highway by PSB officers and the group was ordered to get off the bus. They were subsequently taken to Yinxi PSB station and detained for four nights.

paragraphs.summary: The court states protestors were released after one night; Applicant vowed to continue; detained for four nights en route to provincial government.

propositions.text: Applicant admitted trip was to complain about provincial government corruption; was beaten, threatened with jail, released after two days, and made to sign no-protest documents.
propositions.quote: When asked about the purpose of their trip, the Applicant admitted that they were going to complain about the provincial government’s corruption. The Applicant was subsequently beaten by officers and threatened with jail. They were released two days later and made to sign documents stating that they would no longer protest.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant admitted the trip's purpose, was beaten, threatened, released after two days, and forced to sign no-protest documents.

propositions.text: Applicant beaten for not reporting whereabouts; warned to stop anti-government speeches; fled China late 2017; PSB sought him and threatened wife.
propositions.quote: The Applicant then had to report to the local Town Government where he was beaten for not having the details of his whereabouts every day for the past month. The Applicant was warned again that he must not make any anti-government speeches. The Applicant fled China in late, 2017. His wife received a call shortly after that the PSB had been looking for her husband. They asked that the Applicant report to the police station without delay, otherwise he would be punished severely. A summons was also left with his wife. The PSB allegedly attended his house three more times and threatened his wife if she did not reveal his whereabouts.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant was beaten for not reporting, warned, fled China, and PSB threatened his wife seeking his whereabouts.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant is not wanted by Chinese authorities for protesting farmland expropriation.
propositions.quote: In conducting an independent assessment of the evidence provided by the Applicant, the RAD found that the Applicant is not wanted by Chinese authorities for protesting the expropriation of his farmland.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant did not establish on balance of probabilities involvement in protests, arrests, monthly check-ins, or being sought by authorities.
propositions.quote: The RAD also found that the Applicant has not established that, on a balance of probabilities, that he was involved in protests against the government, arrested twice, required to check in monthly with authorities, and that he is still being sought out.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the Applicant is not wanted by Chinese authorities and did not prove protest involvement, arrests, check-ins, or being sought.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant's documents only show expropriation of some village land, not specifically his leased land; evidence given little weight.
propositions.quote: The RAD found documents provided by the Applicant could only attest to “information regarding the expropriation of some leased land in the village, but not specifically the land leased by the Appellant.” The RAD did acknowledge that the document indicated that the local government intended to expropriate leased land in the area but noted that the Applicant had not provide additional documentation, such as the lease agreement to show the exact location of the property. As such, this evidence was given little weight.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the Applicant's documents did not specifically prove his land was expropriated and gave them little weight.

propositions.text: RAD found unclear to whom prisoner visitor cards relate; Applicant's statements about cards inconsistent and evolving, harming credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD found there was a lack of clarity regarding to whom the prisoner cards relate. The Applicant’s statement that they were the cards for the three chosen representatives ran in contravention of his oral testimony, which provided that the cards were for other individuals who had attended the protest. The RAD also noted that the Applicant’s narrative, which stated that the three chosen representatives were continually detained after their arrest in December 2017 and barred from receiving visitors, was inconsistent with the issuance of the visitor cards themselves. As such, the RAD found the Applicant’s evidence on these documents evolving and internally inconsistent, which draws a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: RAD affirmed RPD's finding that prisoner cards have little weight in proving Applicant protested or is sought by PSB.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the RAD affirmed the RPD’s finding that these documents could be assigned little weight in establishing the Applicant’s allegations he protested against the government and is being sought out by the PSB.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the prisoner cards unclear and inconsistent with Applicant's testimony, harming credibility and giving little weight to the evidence.

propositions.text: RPD noted Applicant lacked credibility for no corroborating letter from wife; Applicant's evidence about wife's letter was evolving and unclear.
propositions.quote: The RPD panel had noted that the Applicant lacked credibility in his testimony about why he had not had a corroborating letter or affidavit from his wife, given her knowledge of the events that took place. The Applicant stated that his wife did write a letter in 2019, but that he had not received it as it had been taken by customs. The RAD found the Applicant’s evidence to be evolving regarding whether his wife had written a letter. During his testimony, the RAD pointed out, the Applicant first stated had not asked his wife to write a letter. Then, upon questioning from his Counsel, the Applicant stated that his wife wrote a letter in 2019, but he did not receive it. The Applicant stated that attempts to reacquire the letter would have been “dangerous”. The Applicant was also not able to clearly articulate how he knew the letter had been taken by customs.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD and RAD found the Applicant lacked credibility about a corroborating letter from his wife, with evolving and unclear evidence.

propositions.text: RAD noted Applicant left China with own passport, obtained Canadian visa fraudulently; exit stamp present; unclear how PSB unaware of exit.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted the Applicant left China using his own passport with help provided by a smuggler to acquire a Canadian visa through fraudulent means. His passport contained an exit stamp from China.

propositions.text: RAD found integrated police database in China would make authorities aware of Applicant's exit; inconsistent with claim PSB sought him after departure.
propositions.quote: Given that he used his own passport, the RAD is unclear how the PSB would not be aware he had left the country, because an integrated database – the Golden Shield - exists which is accessible to all police authorities in China. The RAD found Chinese authorities would have been aware of his exit from China. The RAD suggested this was not consistent with the Applicant’s narrative that Chinese authorities continued to seek him and issued a summons for him after he left China.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the Applicant's use of his own passport and China's police database make it unlikely PSB was unaware of his exit, inconsistent with his claim.

propositions.text: The determinative issue is whether procedural fairness was breached.
propositions.quote: In my view, the determinative issue is this case is procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the key issue is whether procedural fairness was breached.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness questions are reviewed on correctness standard, citing Khosa and other cases.
propositions.quote: Questions of procedural fairness are reviewed on the correctness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, per Binnie J at para 43.

propositions.text: Correctness review may be respectful of decision-maker's choices with some deference, citing Bergeron and Re: Sound.
propositions.quote: ...a correctness review may need to take place in “a manner ‘respectful of the [decision-maker’s] choices’ with ‘a degree of deference’: Re: Sound v Fitness Industry Council of Canada, 2014 FCA 48, 455 N.R. 87 at paragraph 42.”

propositions.text: Judicial review of procedural fairness issues is correctness standard, citing Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers.
propositions.quote: ...judicial review of procedural fairness issues is conducted on the correctness standard: see Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v. Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FCA 196 per de Montigny JA [Near and LeBlanc JJA concurring]: [35] Neither Vavilov nor, for that matter, Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 190, have addressed the standard for determining whether the decision-maker complied with the duty of procedural fairness. In those circumstances, I prefer to rely on the long line of jurisprudence, both from the Supreme Court and from this Court, according to which the standard of review with respect to procedural fairness remains correctness.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains procedural fairness questions are reviewed on correctness standard, citing relevant case law.

propositions.text: Vavilov confirms standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness.
propositions.quote: I also understand from the Supreme Court of Canada’s teaching in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at para 23 that the standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness: [23] Where a court reviews the merits of an administrative decision... the standard of review it applies must reflect the legislature’s intent... The starting point... is a presumption... reasonableness. [Emphasis added]

paragraphs.summary: The court states Vavilov confirms procedural fairness standard of review is correctness.

propositions.text: Dunsmuir explains correctness standard means no deference; court substitutes its own view if it disagrees.
propositions.quote: In Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 50, the Supreme Court of Canada explains what is required of a court reviewing on the correctness standard of review: [50] When applying the correctness standard, a reviewing court will not show deference to the decision maker’s reasoning process; it will rather undertake its own analysis of the question. The analysis will bring the court to decide whether it agrees with the determination of the decision maker; if not, the court will substitute its own view and provide the correct answer. From the outset, the court must ask whether the tribunal’s decision was correct.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Dunsmuir explaining correctness review means no deference and court substitutes its own view if disagreeing.

propositions.text: RAD's central finding was that Applicant's use of own passport and exit stamp means authorities knew he left China; he did not prove authorities sought him after departure.
propositions.quote: Although he has argued that the authorities are not aware that he had left China, I note that he left the country using his own passport. According to the Schedule 12 form, the help provided by the smuggler was to acquire a Canadian visa through fraudulent means. His testimony at the hearing regarding what else the smuggler did for him was vague and ultimately, he stated that he did show his passport to the authorities on more than one occasion. I note that the passport contains an exit stamp from China. Given that he used his own passport, it is unclear how the PSB in China would not be aware that he had exited the country, as an integrated database exists which is accessible to all police authorities in the country. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the authorities would have been aware of his exit from China. I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the authorities sought him out and issued a summons for him after he left China.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD's central finding that authorities knew Applicant left China and he did not prove they sought him after departure.

propositions.text: The RAD's statement that the Applicant argued authorities were unaware he left using his own passport is inaccurate.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points to the RAD’s statement that he “argued that the authorities are not aware he left this country using his own passport”. The Applicant says this statement is not accurate. I agree.

propositions.text: No evidence was shown that the Applicant raised the passport issue before the RAD.
propositions.quote: With respect, I was pointed to no evidence of the Applicant raising this issue before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's statement about the Applicant's passport argument inaccurate and no evidence shows the Applicant raised it before the RAD.

propositions.text: The RAD breached procedural fairness by not allowing the Applicant to respond to a new significant credibility finding.
propositions.quote: Secondly, and fundamentally, the RAD breached procedural fairness by not giving the Applicant a chance to respond to its new and significant credibility finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD breached procedural fairness by not allowing the Applicant to respond to a new credibility finding.

propositions.text: Corvil v Canada (MCI), 2019 FC 300 is the leading authority on procedural fairness in this context.
propositions.quote: With respect, the leading authority in this connection is Corvil v Canada (MCI), 2019 FC 300 [Corvil] [per Leblanc J, as he was then] which has been cited and applied in the Court’s subsequent jurisprudence on many if not most occasions with this type of procedural fairness argument arises.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies Corvil v Canada as the leading authority on procedural fairness here.

propositions.text: When credibility is central, the RAD can make independent findings without questioning the applicant or giving another chance to respond.
propositions.quote: it is now a well-established fact that when the credibility of a refugee protection claimant is at the heart of the RPD’s decision and the grounds for appeal before the RAD, the RAD is entitled to make independent findings in this regard, without having to question the applicant or giving the applicant another opportunity to make submissions.

propositions.text: The RAD must notify parties and allow response if considering questions not raised before the RPD or parties.
propositions.quote: when considering a question which was not raised before the RPD or by any of the parties to the appeal, the RAD must first notify the parties accordingly and give them an opportunity to respond thereto

propositions.text: The RAD must avoid disregarding contradictory evidence or making findings on evidence unknown to the applicant.
propositions.quote: the RAD must avoid disregarding contradictory evidence on the record or making findings based on evidence unknown to the applicant

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Corvil's rules on RAD's independent findings and procedural fairness requirements.

propositions.text: Whether the Applicant’s credibility was central to the RPD’s decision and the RAD’s grounds for appeal.
propositions.quote: the issue resolves into whether the Applicant’s credibility was at the heart of the RPD’s decision and the grounds for appeal before the RAD.

propositions.text: The precondition that credibility was central is not met despite RPD saying credibility was determinative.
propositions.quote: While I agree the RPD said in its reasons the Applicant’s credibility was determinative that to my mind is not the end of this issue for several reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court questions if credibility was central to the RPD decision and RAD appeal grounds, finding the precondition unmet.

propositions.text: The passport issue was not raised before the RPD, which made no reference to it or its consequences.
propositions.quote: The passport issue was not raised before the RPD. Indeed, the RPD made no reference to the passport issue and its consequences.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the passport issue was not raised or referenced before the RPD.

propositions.text: Judicial review focuses on the RAD decision and what was before it.
propositions.quote: on this judicial review we are looking at the RAD and its decision, i.e., what was before the RAD and the impact of the RAD’s decision on the case.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes judicial review concerns the RAD decision and its record.

propositions.text: The passport issue was not raised in written submissions before the RAD.
propositions.quote: Notably, the passport issue was not raised before the RAD in written submissions.

propositions.text: No evidence suggests the RAD raised the passport issue during hearings with parties and counsel.
propositions.quote: I was given nothing to suggest the RAD raised the passport issue when the parties and counsel were before it.

propositions.text: If the RAD raised the issue during or after hearing, it should have given procedural fairness notice to parties.
propositions.quote: If the issue arose then, it should have been raised with the parties. If it occurred after the hearing, it could and should have been canvassed in some form of procedural fairness notice.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the passport issue was not raised before the RAD and procedural fairness notice was required if it was.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded the credibility issue was central to the RPD’s decision.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded the issue of credibility was at the heart of the RPD’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not convinced credibility was central to the RPD decision.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded credibility was central to the RAD’s grounds for appeal, which focused on documentary evidence and persecution assessment.
propositions.quote: I am certainly not persuaded the issue of credibility was at the heart of the grounds for appeal before the RAD, which were a) did the Board err in assessing Mr. Yu’s documentary evidence? b) did the Board err in assessing whether Mr. Yu faced persecution due to his political activities?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds credibility was not central to the RAD appeal grounds, which concerned documentary evidence and persecution.

propositions.text: The passport issue was a new issue not raised before the RPD or RAD.
propositions.quote: the passport issue and its consequences was a new issue not raised before either the RPD or the RAD.

propositions.text: The RAD made a credibility finding and consequential findings based on this new issue.
propositions.quote: the RAD, in addition, made a credibility finding having set out the issue as it did, and in addition made consequential findings in terms of other evidence before it as a result.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the passport issue was new and the RAD made credibility and consequential findings based on it.

propositions.text: The new argument's impact should be disregarded as other unchallenged credibility findings suffice to find the Applicant not credible.
propositions.quote: I am asked in effect to disregard the raising, determination and assessment of the impact of this new argument on the Applicant’s case because in effect it would not make any difference, since there were many other unchallenged credibility findings which were more than sufficient to find the Applicant not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the new argument's impact should be disregarded due to other sufficient credibility findings.

propositions.text: Disregarding the new argument requires reassessing material evidence, which is improper for this Court.
propositions.quote: In response the Applicant correctly notes this would entail my reassessing material evidence: I agree.

propositions.text: The new credibility finding was material and important, involving factual issues for the RAD to decide, not this Court.
propositions.quote: In my view this was a material and important finding. Such a reassessment would necessarily include the presence or absence of alleged summons, what if any efforts the PSB were or were not making to find the Applicant after he left, whether and to what extent the Applicant used a smuggler, and perhaps other factual issues. These are for the RAD not this Court to make.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues reassessment is improper; the court agrees the new finding is material and for the RAD to decide.

propositions.text: Corvil allows RAD independent findings without notice but requires notice if considering questions not raised before RPD or parties.
propositions.quote: Corvil is a double-edged sword. While it sets out when the RAD may make independent factual findings without notice, it also sets out that when considering a question not raised before the RPD or by any of the parties to the appeal, the RAD must first notify the parties accordingly and give them an opportunity to respond thereto.

propositions.text: The RAD did not notify the parties or give an opportunity to respond regarding the new issue in this case.
propositions.quote: This did not occur in the case at hand.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Corvil's dual rule and finds the RAD failed to notify parties or allow response here.

propositions.text: The procedural fairness issue determines the appeal; other issues need not be addressed.
propositions.quote: Given this procedural issue determines this appeal, there is no need to deal with the other issues raised.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the procedural fairness issue decides the appeal, so other issues are unnecessary to address.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is granted.
propositions.quote: For the reasons above, the Application for judicial review will be granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: No question of general importance arises or is certified.
propositions.quote: Neither party proposed a question of general importance, and none arises.

propositions.text: The judicial review is granted, the matter remanded to a differently constituted decision-maker, no costs order made.
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT in IMM-7035-21 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the application for judicial review is granted, the matter is remanded for redetermination by a differently constituted decision-maker, no question of general importance is certified, and there is no Order as to costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, remands the matter, declines certification, and orders no costs.
